questions.question: After `a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3)`, what is the value of `a`?
questions.explanation: Assignment binds a second name to the same list object; mutating it through b is visible through a.

questions.question: When should you use `is` instead of `==`?
options: When comparing singletons such as None, True, False or sentinel objects
When comparing any two integers, because it is faster
When comparing strings of equal length
questions.explanation: `is` checks identity and is only reliable for singletons; value comparison should use `==`.

questions.question: Why is `hash(([1], 2))` an error?
options: Tuples are mutable and therefore unhashable
Tuples can only be hashed if they have exactly one element
The tuple contains a list, which is unhashable, so the tuple is unhashable too
questions.explanation: A tuple is hashable only if all of its elements are hashable; a contained list makes it unhashable even though the tuple itself is immutable.

questions.question: Why might `a is b` be True for `256` but False for two separately created `1000` values in CPython?
options: Python guarantees that all integers below 1000 are singletons
CPython caches small integers from -5 to 256 as an implementation detail
Large integers are stored as floats
`is` compares values only for small numbers
questions.explanation: Small-int caching is a CPython implementation detail, not a language guarantee, which is why `is` must never be used to compare numbers.
